title: Silica Aerogel Matrix
description: Signature original design. Signature design: a graded-pore aerogel with wide intake pores narrowing to molecular traps, so vapor flows in freely but water clusters cannot escape before harvest. Silica aerogels are ultra-porous solids that are up to 99.8% air by volume, giving them enormous internal surface area for vapor adsorption. Their nanoscale pore network traps water molecules from passing air even at low relative humidity. Key Signature facts: Surface areas reach 500 to 1000 square meters per gram, far above conventional desiccants; Thermal conductivity near 0.015 watts per meter-kelvin keeps captured heat where it is needed; and Hydrophobic surface treatments prevent liquid flooding of the nanopores.

title: MOF-Enhanced Aerogel Composites
description: Signature original design. Signature design: MOF crystals grown directly inside the aerogel during gelation, forming a single monolith instead of a glued laminate. Metal-organic frameworks such as MOF-801 and MOF-303 can be embedded in aerogel sheets to add sharp, low-humidity water uptake steps. These crystalline cages adsorb water steeply even below 20 percent relative humidity, where plain silica underperforms. Key Signature facts: MOF-303 adsorbs about 0.48 grams of water per gram at low humidity in published tests; Composite sheets keep the MOF crystals fixed so they survive thousands of wet-dry cycles; and Day-night cycling uses cool night air for capture and warm day air for release.

title: Hygroscopic Salt Impregnation
description: Signature original design. Signature design: salt sealed in microcapsules inside the aerogel so only vapor, never liquid brine, reaches the outer surface. Salts such as lithium chloride and calcium chloride can be loaded into aerogel pores to boost uptake through deliquescence. The salt dissolves into captured vapor and keeps pulling moisture long after the bare surface would saturate. Key Signature facts: LiCl-loaded composites have reported uptakes above 1.5 grams of water per gram of sorbent; Pore confinement stops the liquid salt from leaking or clumping between cycles; and Regeneration needs only moderate heat, roughly 60 to 80 degrees Celsius.

description: Signature original design. Signature design: a honeycomb paper frame that folds flat for shipping and springs open into a rigid sorbent panel on site. title: Sorption Bed Geometry
description: Signature original design. Signature design: wedge-shaped beds that are thin at the air inlet and thicker downstream, matching the falling humidity gradient. The sorbent bed is shaped as thin panels or corrugated stacks so that night air sweeps across maximum surface with minimum fan power. Thin beds saturate faster and release water faster when heated, tightening the daily cycle. Key Signature facts: Beds 5 to 15 millimeters thick balance airflow resistance against sorbent mass; Corrugation doubles exposed area inside the same enclosure volume; and Modular panels let a damaged sheet be swapped without tools.

title: Passive Radiative Cooling Panels
description: Signature original design. Signature design: a radiative panel that flips at dawn — sky-facing cooler by night, solar absorber by day for the release step. Panels that radiate heat to the cold night sky can drop several degrees below ambient air, pre-chilling intake air and raising relative humidity at the sorbent surface. This is entirely passive, using selective infrared emitters. Key Signature facts: Night-sky cooling can reach 5 to 10 degrees Celsius below ambient in clear desert skies; Higher relative humidity at the sorbent multiplies uptake without extra energy; and Daytime the same panels shade the bed from direct sun.

title: Condenser Surfaces
description: Signature original design. Signature design: condenser fins shaped like pine needles, so droplets grow, merge, and self-eject into the gutter. title: Diurnal Cycle Control
description: Signature original design. Signature design: a bimetallic latch that seals the bed automatically when the panel warms past the crossover point — no electronics. The harvester runs a daily rhythm: adsorb through the cool night, then seal and heat the bed after sunrise to drive water off. Timing the switch to the humidity and temperature crossover maximizes daily yield. Key Signature facts: Adsorption typically runs from dusk to mid-morning, about 10 to 12 hours; Desorption completes in 2 to 4 hours of morning heat; and Smart timing can add 15 to 25 percent more water per day.

description: Signature original design. Signature design: a coin-slot liter meter — the unit pays for itself drop by drop, owned by the village from day one. Levelized cost per liter decides adoption: hardware amortized over life plus consumables, divided by lifetime water. Current designs target well under bottled-water prices. Key Signature facts: Hardware target under 150 dollars per household unit at volume; Levelized cost goal below 0.10 dollars per liter; and Pay-as-you-harvest metering can finance units for the poorest users.

demo.program:
# cost demo -- Cost and Finance Model
# field: Deployment and Scale

capex = 150
opex_yr = 12
life_yr = 7
out_yr = 1200
out_u = "liters"
lifetime = capex + opex_yr * life_yr
total_out = out_yr * life_yr
print('Lifetime cost: $%.4g' % lifetime)
print('Lifetime output: %.4g %s' % (total_out, out_u))
print('Cost per %s: $%.4g' % (out_u, lifetime / total_out))

title: Village-Scale Integration
description: Signature original design. Signature design: the kiosk is also the school charging station — water, light, and power from one village hub. Arrays of units feed a central kiosk with larger storage, treatment, and distribution. Shared maintenance and bulk spares make the economics work where single units would not. Key Signature facts: 20 units feed a 400-liter central tank for a small village; One trained caretaker maintains the whole array; and Kiosk sales of surplus water fund replacement parts.
